title: Japan Declares Combat Drones Essential, Pentagon Signs $3B Interceptor Deal, Russia Floats New Nuclear Sub
subhead: Japan's defense white paper makes drones and AI a national priority as the Pentagon races to replenish Patriot and THAAD stockpiles drained by the Iran and Ukraine wars. Russia floats its latest Yasen-M submarine as Ukraine's naval drones evolve into FPV motherships.

sections.heading: Japan Declares Combat Drones Essential in Defense White Paper
sections.body:
Japan's Cabinet adopted a 598-page annual defense paper on Tuesday that identifies low-cost combat drones and AI as essential to adapting to 'new ways of warfare' demonstrated in Ukraine and the Middle East. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said 'speed is key' as the country races to close capability gaps against China's rapidly expanding military.

The paper reiterates that China remains Japan's biggest strategic challenge, citing the growing presence and frequency of Chinese warships in the Pacific. Japan's Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency has already selected four drone makers from 38 applicants for a rapid development program, with navy testing scheduled for early August before a final selection. Toshiba separately announced plans to jointly develop combat drones with startup Pro Drone.

The white paper also reframes Japan's military buildup as an economic opportunity. A companion Reuters report notes that Tokyo is now portraying defense spending not just as a deterrent but as a path to greater prosperity, arguing that a robust domestic defense industry can drive industrial growth. This messaging shift comes as Japan's defense budget continues its climb toward the NATO-standard 2% of GDP target.

The drone push addresses a structural constraint: Japan's shrinking population is reducing available military manpower, making unmanned systems a necessity rather than a luxury. But the country faces a challenge in developing indigenous drones when its commercial drone market is dominated by Chinese imports, according to AP reporting.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is moving from defense debate to defense production. The rapid drone development program — from 38 applicants down to 4 in months — shows Tokyo is compressing procurement timelines in ways that mirror US Replicator-style urgency. If Japan successfully builds a domestic combat drone industry, it could become a significant drone exporter in Asia.

sections.heading: Pentagon Signs $3B+ Deal to Ramp Up Patriot and THAAD Production
sections.body:
The US Defense Department signed a framework deal worth more than $3 billion with Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman on Monday to expand production capacity for Patriot and THAAD interceptor missile components, according to Reuters. The move comes as the Iran war and Ukraine conflict have strained US missile interceptor stockpiles to critical levels.

Separate reporting indicates the Pentagon aims to triple Patriot missile production and quadruple THAAD interceptor production through the framework agreement. Northrop Grumman signed deals worth $3 billion to supply rocket motors and THAAD components specifically.

The scale of the stockpile drawdown is stark: analysts estimate US Patriot interceptor stocks have fallen from about 2,300 to under 1,000 as interceptors have been deployed to the Middle East and transferred to Ukraine. Rebuilding those inventories is likely to take years even with expanded production lines.

The deal reflects a Pentagon that has moved from contingency planning to industrial mobilization. The framework structure allows the military to place orders without renegotiating contracts each time, compressing procurement timelines. But even with the expanded capacity, the production ramp means significant interceptors won't reach stockpiles until 2027-2028 at the earliest.
sections.whyItMatters: The $3B interceptor deal is the latest sign that the Iran war has turned US munitions replenishment from a future planning problem into an immediate production crisis. With Patriot stocks under 1,000 interceptors, the US is running on fumes in two theaters simultaneously. The framework deal structure — rather than individual contracts — signals the Pentagon has shifted to wartime procurement logic.

sections.heading: Germany Approves €800M in Arms Exports to Israel, Mostly for Nuclear-Capable Submarine
sections.body:
Germany has approved nearly €800 million ($913 million) in arms export licences to Israel in the first five months of 2026 alone — more than in the previous 20 months combined, according to a German government response to a parliamentary question by the AfD party reported by Al Jazeera.

More than 60% of the total value is earmarked for a single unnamed 'major maritime project' that analysts identified as the INS Drakon, a Dolphin II-class submarine built by German manufacturer TKMS. The submarine underwent its maiden voyage last year at a shipyard in Kiel and was officially handed over to the Israeli Navy last week, according to German media.

The Drakon is believed to feature a vertical launching system (VLS) capable of firing nuclear-tipped cruise missiles or ballistic missiles, making Israel only the second navy after South Korea known to field VLS on an AIP-equipped conventional submarine. The vessel would provide Israel a sea-based nuclear second-strike capability.

TKMS separately signed a memorandum of understanding with Elbit Systems, Israel's largest private defense contractor, for future collaboration. TKMS was also selected by Canada as preferred bidder to build up to 12 submarines in what would be the largest order in TKMS history, valued at €12-18 billion.

The surge in approvals comes despite Berlin's stated concern about Israel's military conduct in Gaza. Chancellor Merz announced a suspension of weapons licences for Israel in August 2025, lifted it in November, and the current approvals show a dramatic acceleration.
sections.whyItMatters: Germany is subsidizing roughly 30% of Israel's submarine costs while officially expressing concern about Gaza — a contradiction that's becoming harder to sustain. The INS Drakon's VLS capability represents a qualitative leap in Israel's nuclear deterrent, and TKMS's Canadian deal shows how German submarine expertise is becoming a NATO-wide strategic asset.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Magura Naval Drones Evolve Into FPV Motherships, Strike Russian Radar in Crimea
sections.body:
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) announced that its Magura V7 naval platforms have struck Russian radar targets on land in occupied Crimea for the first time, marking a significant evolution in the drone's combat role.

The operation, carried out by HUR's Group 13 special unit in late July, used Magura platforms carrying FPV (first-person-view) drones to destroy a command vehicle belonging to a Podlet radar system and a Parol-4 identification friend-or-foe interrogator. HUR said this was the first time the platforms had launched FPV drones against ground targets.

'From now on, our Maguras threaten the Russian occupiers on land as well — this fundamentally shifts the fight into a new dimension,' HUR stated. Previously, Group 13 had destroyed nine Russian vessels and damaged five using Magura drones, along with three helicopters and two fighter jets.

The development is operationally significant: naval drones that can launch FPV kamikaze drones against coastal targets expand Ukraine's strike envelope well beyond ship-to-ship engagements. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has already been forced to withdraw most major vessels from Crimean ports, and the new capability means even shore-based radar and air defense systems are now vulnerable to sea-launched drone attacks.
sections.whyItMatters: The Magura V7's FPV mothership capability transforms Ukraine's naval drones from anti-ship weapons into multi-domain strike platforms. This is a doctrinal innovation — cheap naval vessels acting as drone carriers — that other navies will study closely. It also means Russia can no longer assume that moving air defenses inland from the coast provides safety.

sections.heading: Russia Floats Ulyanovsk Nuclear Submarine, Prepares Admiral Nakhimov Cruiser for Trials
sections.body:
Russia's Sevmash Shipyard has floated out the Ulyanovsk, a Project 885M (Yasen-M) nuclear-powered cruise missile submarine, marking the latest addition to Russia's fourth-generation submarine fleet. The Yasen-M class features reduced acoustic signatures and can carry long-range, high-precision missiles capable of striking land, sea, and underwater targets, according to TASS reporting.

Sevmash CEO Mikhail Budnichenko confirmed that the shipyard will deliver two vessels to the Russian Navy by year end. The Yasen-M submarine Perm, laid down in 2016 and launched in March 2025, is scheduled to complete all testing stages this year.

In parallel, the Project 1144.2M heavy nuclear-powered cruiser Admiral Nakhimov — under modernization since 2013 and in repair since 1999 — is set for 2.5 months of sea trials. The modernized cruiser will reportedly carry 10 universal naval launch systems, each capable of deploying eight Kalibr-NK and/or Oniks cruise missiles, dramatically increasing its striking power.

Despite sanctions and production challenges, Russia's naval shipbuilding program is showing resilience. Sevmash has delivered 14 nuclear submarines over the past 14 years, maintaining a roughly one-per-year cadence even under wartime conditions.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is keeping its naval nuclear program on track despite the war in Ukraine and Western sanctions. The Yasen-M class is the backbone of Russia's modern attack submarine fleet, and the Admiral Nakhimov's modernization — with 80 cruise missile cells — would give Russia's Northern Fleet a significant surface combatant capability for the first time in decades.

sections.heading: Defense Tech VC Funding Hits $32B Since 2022 as Pentagon Opens Doors to Startups
sections.body:
Venture capitalists have poured a record $32 billion into defense tech companies since 2022, according to PitchBook data reported by Forbes, with $12.8 billion invested in just the first half of 2026 — more than five times the total for all of 2022. The number of defense companies founded annually has nearly quadrupled since 2022, and Y Combinator incubated 32 defense startups last year, up eightfold since 2020.

The boom is producing outsized valuations. Shield AI is now worth $12.7 billion after its March fundraising, with over $400 million in revenue. Its V-BAT drones are being used by Ukraine, Japan, and the US. Palmer Luckey's Anduril has reached $11.9 billion in funding, and naval drone maker Saronic has raised $2.6 billion.

The shift reflects a Pentagon that is actively opening its doors to nontraditional contractors. According to CSIS, 'nontraditional' firms received $122.6 billion in defense contract commitments in 2025, double the amount from a decade earlier. Some 10,000 new businesses have joined the defense industrial base in the past two years. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll predicted VC investment in defense will 'triple or quadruple' in coming years.

US lawmakers approved an $839 billion defense spending bill for 2026, a 15% increase over 2022, and Trump has proposed $1.1 trillion for 2027. The funding pipeline is enormous, but the question remains whether startups can scale production fast enough to matter in active conflicts.
sections.whyItMatters: The defense industry's center of gravity is shifting. The 'Big Five' primes (Boeing, General Dynamics, Lockheed, Northrop, RTX) still dominate major platforms, but the explosion of VC-backed startups is creating a parallel industrial base that moves faster and builds cheaper. Whether Shield AI's V-BATs or Saronic's naval drones can scale to wartime production volumes remains the open question.

sections.heading: Asia's Defense Spending Headed Toward $1.2 Trillion by 2030
sections.body:
Asia's defense spending is projected to rise from roughly $700 billion in 2026 to $1-1.2 trillion by 2030, according to analysis by WisdomTree cited by Seeking Alpha, with capital flowing toward drones, ships, missiles, and defense electronics. Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and India are all accelerating defense investment through domestic manufacturing, advanced technologies, and exports.

The spending surge is being driven by a convergence of threats: China's naval expansion, North Korean missile provocations, and the demonstration effect of drone warfare in Ukraine and the Middle East. Japan's defense white paper released this week is the latest example of how Asian governments are framing military spending as both a security necessity and an economic opportunity.

Suppliers of electronics, specialty materials, propellants, and batteries stand to gain alongside prime contractors, broadening the investment landscape beyond traditional aerospace and naval firms.
sections.whyItMatters: Asia's defense spending trajectory — a 60-70% increase in four years — is reshaping the global defense market. The region is moving from being primarily a US arms customer to building its own industrial base, with Japan and South Korea emerging as significant exporters. This shifts procurement leverage away from Western primes and creates new competitive dynamics.

bottomLine: Japan's defense white paper making combat drones an urgent national priority and the Pentagon's $3B interceptor deal with Lockheed and Northrop Grumman both reflect the same reality: the wars in Iran and Ukraine have turned procurement timelines from years into months. Germany's €800M in arms exports to Israel — mostly for a nuclear-capable submarine — shows that strategic arms transfers continue regardless of political rhetoric. Meanwhile, Ukraine's Magura V7 naval drones evolving into FPV motherships demonstrates how fast battlefield innovation is moving, and Russia's continued submarine deliveries confirm that sanctions have not stopped its naval nuclear program. The global defense industrial base is expanding — $32B in VC funding and 10,000 new entrants in two years — but the question is whether speed of innovation can translate into speed of production.
sources: Reuters, AP News, Al Jazeera, Forbes, Seeking Alpha, TASS, Kyiv Independent, Defense News, BBC, PitchBook, WisdomTree, CSIS, Breaking Defense, MSN
